533.title: Luqman's advice to his son
533.hook: Luqman the wise tells his son: don't associate anything with Allah (31:13)
533.howItsDone: Muslim parents and teachers often use Luqman's advice in 31:13–19 as a model for raising children, beginning with tawhid, the oneness of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: aya, the sign in our languages and colors. Your line was difference is a sign. Today, a new surah.

Some advice from a parent arrives at a big moment: leaving home, a wedding, a hospital bed. Some arrives over the washing up, and only years later turns out to have stuck. Surah Luqman, the thirty-first, is named for a man the Qur'an calls wise, and at its heart is a father talking to his son, piece by piece. The Qur'an keeps his words and lets us listen in.

Who was Luqman? The Qur'an says only that God gave him wisdom, hikma, and that wisdom first meant: give thanks to God. Beyond that, the sources are quiet. Later tradition says he was from Africa, perhaps Nubia or Abyssinia, and reports differ on whether he was a tailor, a carpenter or a shepherd. Scholars have asked whether he was a prophet; tradition mostly remembers him as a wise man, and the Qur'an doesn't settle it. What it gives is his words. Pickthall: "O my dear son! Ascribe no partners unto Allah. Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong." Start with ya bunayya: not just ibni, my son, but the small, tender form, my dear boy. The weightiest advice starts with affection. Ascribing partners is shirk: treating anything else, money, power, a person, an idol, as if it shared God's place. Luqman calls it zulm 'azim, a tremendous wrong. The classical dictionaries define zulm as putting something where it doesn't belong. A hadith in Bukhari shows how much this verse mattered. When another verse said safety belongs to those who don't mix their faith with zulm, the companions were frightened: which of us hasn't wronged himself? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them it doesn't mean that; it means what Luqman told his son: shirk is a tremendous wrong. So the first advice puts first things first. Before manners, prayer, or how to walk and talk, which come later in the speech: know who God is, and put nothing in His place.
screen: `WHO WAS LUQMAN? THE QUR'AN IS QUIET.` · `YA BUNAYYA: MY DEAR SON.` · `SHIRK: A TREMENDOUS WRONG.` · `FIRST THINGS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of the best advice anyone ever gave you, the one that actually changed something, and remember who gave it and how; was there tenderness in it? Then think of someone younger or newer who might need it someday, and hear how you'd say it, starting the way Luqman did, with affection. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name.
Luqman. The wise man of surah thirty-one, whose speech to his son starts, my dear son, and puts first: don't ascribe partners to God. Today's word.

534.title: Weakness upon weakness
534.hook: his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, so thank Me and your parents (31:14)
534.howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents, birr al-walidayn, as a major duty that follows directly after the worship of God, and pray for their parents, living or dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Luqman, and his first advice: put nothing in God's place. Your line was the first advice.

The last weeks of a pregnancy. The back that aches whatever you do. Sleeping propped on pillows, getting up again and again in the night. Then the birth. Then the newborn months, feeding through the night on almost no sleep while the body is still recovering. In the middle of Luqman's advice to his son, the Qur'an interrupts, in God's own voice, to say something about exactly that.

Luqman has just told his son not to ascribe partners to God. Then come two verses that aren't Luqman's; they're God speaking. We have enjoined on the human being concerning his parents. Pickthall: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years". Then: give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the journey's end. Weakness upon weakness, wahnan 'ala wahn. Commentators read it as weakness piled on weakness: the strain of pregnancy getting heavier month by month, then birth, then nursing. The verse sees it. Notice the order of thanks: to Me, and to your parents. In one breath, gratitude to God and to the people who carried and raised you are joined. Then the next verse adds a limit. If your parents strive to make you associate with God what you have no knowledge of, don't obey them; and yet keep company with them in this world kindly. Even in disagreement about the most important thing, the kindness stays. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ underlined the mother's place. In a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, a man asks who most deserves his good company. Your mother, the Prophet says. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your father. Some commentators connect the threefold mother to three hardships: carrying, birth, nursing. Not every relationship with a mother is easy, and the verse doesn't say it is. What it asks is that people remember what was carried.
screen: `GOD'S VOICE INSIDE LUQMAN'S.` · `WAHNAN 'ALA WAHN.` · `THANK ME, AND YOUR PARENTS.` · `YOUR MOTHER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Think of your mother, or whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a foster parent, an older sister, and find one specific thing she carried for you that you probably never thanked her for, a night shift, a school run, a meal she skipped. If she's gone, or things are complicated, you can simply hold her in mind kindly. If you pray, you can pray for her.
Wahn. Weakness, the Qur'an's word for what a mother carries, doubled as wahnan 'ala wahn, weakness upon weakness: pregnancy, birth and nursing, strain piled on strain. Today's word.
Your line: remember what was carried. Kindness stays, even where things are hard. See you tomorrow.

535.title: Walk modestly, lower your voice
535.hook: don't turn your cheek in scorn, walk modestly, lower your voice (31:18–19)
535.howItsDone: Muslims often teach Luqman's last pieces of advice, 31:17–19, as a short guide to manners: prayer, patience, humility, a moderate walk and a lowered voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wahn, weakness upon weakness, what a mother carries. Your line was remember what was carried.

Some people announce their importance before saying a word. They take up the middle of the corridor. They half-turn their face away when someone they consider beneath them starts talking. They take the phone call at full volume in the train carriage. Luqman's advice to his son ends not with doctrine but with exactly this: how to hold your face, how to walk, and how loud to be.

Luqman has told his son to pray, to enjoin what's right, to forbid what's wrong, and to be patient with what befalls him. Then he gets physical. Pickthall: "Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land." The Arabic for turning the cheek is tusa''ir khaddak. Classical lexicons say sa'ar was a condition in camels that made them twist their necks to one side. So picture a head permanently turned away from others, as if they're not worth facing. Walking with pertness is marahan: strutting, walking in exultation. God doesn't love, the verse says, every arrogant boaster. Then the positive version. Pickthall: "Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice." The first word is iqsid, from the same root as qasd, the middle, moderation: not crawling, not strutting, a steady pace aimed somewhere. And lower your voice, ughdud, the same verb the Qur'an uses for lowering the gaze. Then a line that sticks: the harshest of all voices is the braying of the donkey. Loudness for its own sake isn't strength; it's noise. This isn't a rule against ever raising your voice. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called out to warn, and the call to prayer is meant to carry. It's about posture toward people: a face that turns toward them, a walk that doesn't take over the street, and a voice sized to the room.
screen: `TURN NOT THY CHEEK IN SCORN.` · `NO STRUTTING IN THE LAND.` · `IQSID: THE STEADY MIDDLE PACE.` · `LOWER YOUR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Notice your face right now, whether it's turned toward anything or away, and let it soften. Then bring to mind the place where you're usually loudest, the kitchen, a meeting, the car, a group chat in capital letters, and replay that moment with your voice at half and your face toward the other person. If you pray, you can ask for a gentle voice.
Walk modestly. Luqman's advice on how to carry yourself: don't turn your cheek in scorn, don't strut, keep a steady pace, and lower your voice. Today's word.
Your line: lower your voice. Gentleness can still be heard. Day five hundred thirty-five, done.

536.title: If the sea were ink
536.hook: if every tree were pens and the sea ink, with seven more seas, His words would not run out (31:27)
536.howItsDone: Muslims often recite 31:27 and 18:109 when speaking of the vastness of God's knowledge and words, and calligraphers have written the verse many times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: walk modestly, Luqman's advice on face, pace and voice. Your line was lower your voice.

Before printing, writing was physical. A calligrapher cut a pen from a reed, sharpened it with a knife, dipped, wrote a few words, dipped again. Ink was ground and mixed by hand, and it ran out. A copy of the Qur'an could take months. Every scribe knew the pot running dry halfway through a line. Near its end, Surah Luqman takes that ordinary scribe's experience and stretches it until it breaks.
screen: `A REED PEN, A KNIFE, A POT OF INK.`

segments.voice: Pickthall: "And if all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to help it, (were ink), the words of Allah could not be exhausted. Lo! Allah is Mighty, Wise." Picture it. Every forest, every orchard, every palm, cut into aqlam, reed pens. The ocean as the ink pot, and seven more oceans poured in behind it. The scribes write and write, the pens wear down, the seas go dry, and the words of God are still not finished. Pickthall puts were ink in brackets because the Arabic leaves it out; the picture is clear enough without it. Surah Al-Kahf has a shorter version of the image: if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would run out before His words did, even if We brought another like it. What are the words? Commentators gave several answers: His knowledge, which has no edge; His commands, the be! by which everything comes into being; His wonders in creation, which no one could ever finish describing. Seven, in Arabic, often works as a number of abundance, not a precise count. The verse isn't measuring; it's overwhelming. And it says something about every book, every sermon, every lesson, including this one: they're a few drops from that sea. Whatever has been said about God, there's always more. For many Muslims that isn't a frustration but a comfort: the source never runs dry.
screen: `EVERY TREE ON EARTH, A PEN.` · `THE SEA, AND SEVEN MORE, AS INK.` · `HIS KNOWLEDGE, COMMANDS AND WONDERS.` · `A FEW DROPS FROM THAT SEA.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing in the world that amazes you, the color of a sky, a child's laugh, the way a wound closes, and find one word for it, on a scrap of paper or held in mind. Look at the word, notice how much more there is that it doesn't say, and let that feel like abundance, not failure. If you pray, you can say subhan Allah over it.

537.title: Leaving their beds
537.hook: they forsake their beds to call on their Lord in fear and hope (32:16)
537.howItsDone: Many Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer, in the last part of the night before the dawn prayer, especially in Ramadan, and many recite Surah As-Sajdah before sleeping.

segments.voice: Yesterday: aqlam, the pens that could never finish God's words. Your line was the words don't run out. Today, a new surah.

There's a particular quiet at about four in the morning. No traffic, no notifications. The fridge hums. A bird tries one note and stops. Shift workers know it, new parents know it, and so do people who get up on purpose, before dawn, to pray. Surah As-Sajdah, the Prostration, the thirty-second, is short, and one of its pictures of the believers is someone alone at night, getting out of a warm bed.

The verse before describes those who, when reminded of God's signs, fall down in prostration; it's one of the places where readers traditionally prostrate as they recite, and the surah is named As-Sajdah. Then the picture. Pickthall: "Who forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope". The Arabic is vivid: tatajafa junubuhum 'an al-madaji', their sides draw away from their beds, as if the body itself pulls back from sleep. And the two words: fear and hope, khawfan wa tama'an. The night prayer holds both, honesty about what's wrong and reaching toward mercy. The practice is called qiyam al-layl, standing in the night. Another name is tahajjud, from a root about sleep; the dictionaries give this form the sense of leaving it. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, explaining to Mu'adh ibn Jabal the doors of good, mentioned prayer in the middle of the night, then recited this very verse. And a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says that in the last third of every night, God descends to the nearest heaven and asks: who is calling on Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking of Me, that I may give him? It's voluntary, not one of the five prayers: a few short units in the dark, as often or as rarely as someone chooses. Another hadith in Tirmidhi reports that the Prophet would not sleep until he had recited this surah. The verse is honest about the cost, a warm bed and a little sleep, and about what it buys: time to call on God in fear and in hope.

Then back to sleep, or into the day.

538.title: Hidden joy
538.hook: no soul knows what joy is kept hidden for them (32:17)
538.howItsDone: Many Muslims value hidden good deeds, such as secret charity and night prayer, and recite 32:17 alongside the hadith of what no eye has seen when speaking of paradise.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qiyam al-layl, standing in the night in fear and hope. Your line was up in the night.

A box handed over with a grin, and the giver says: don't shake it. Half the joy is not knowing. The other half is finding, when you open it, that the giver knew you better than you thought. As-Sajdah has just described people getting up in the dark to pray, unseen. The very next verse says what's waiting for them. Or rather, it says something more interesting: that nobody knows.

Pickthall: "No soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy, as a reward for what they used to do." The phrase Pickthall translates joy is qurrat a'yun, literally coolness of the eyes, an old Arabic idiom. In a hot land, coolness is relief, and an old explanation in the dictionaries says tears of grief are hot, tears of happiness cool. So qurrat 'ayn is what cools your eyes, what makes you deeply, quietly glad. The same idiom appears elsewhere in the Qur'an for spouses and children, and for the baby Musa. Here it's kept hidden: ukhfiya, concealed. A hadith in Bukhari brings the verse to life. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that God says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has never occurred to any human heart. Abu Hurayra, who reported it, added: recite if you wish, no soul knows what is kept hidden for them. Some early commentators noticed a symmetry. The people in the verse before prayed in secret, at night, where no one could see, so their reward is secret too: a hidden deed, answered with a hidden joy. A kind of justice, and a kind of tenderness. The Qur'an gives many pictures of paradise: gardens, rivers, shade, fruit. Read with the hadith, this verse says those pictures fall short: whatever a person imagines, the reward is beyond it. A hope never described, only promised, and kept hidden like the prayer that earned it.

539.title: A beautiful example
539.hook: in the messenger of Allah you have a beautiful example (33:21)
539.carry: do the hard thing with them
539.howItsDone: Muslims follow the sunnah, the Prophet's example, in worship and in daily habits, learning it from the hadith collections and from biographies of his life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hidden joy, qurrat a'yun, kept hidden for those who prayed unseen. Your line was joy kept hidden.

Medina, under threat. A confederacy of tribes is marching on the city. On the advice of Salman the Persian, the biographies say, the Muslims decide to dig a trench across the open side of the city. Men with picks and baskets, in the cold, short on food, racing against time. And among them, carrying earth on his back until the dust covered his skin, the leader of the community. Surah Al-Ahzab, the Confederates, the thirty-third, tells of those days.

The surah describes the fear honestly. Eyes grew wild, hearts reached the throats, and people began to think all kinds of thoughts about God. Some slipped away with excuses. And right in the middle of that account comes the verse. Pickthall: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much." The Arabic is uswatun hasanah. Hasanah is good, beautiful, excellent. Uswah is a model, someone you copy. The verse isn't on a poster. It's in a trench. Bukhari reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ dug and carried earth alongside everyone, chanting verses with them as they worked. Jabir reported that when a huge rock blocked the digging, the Prophet came and broke it, and that he had a stone tied against his stomach from hunger, the same as the rest. The example wasn't in how he talked about hardship. It was in doing the hardship with them. That's what Muslims mean by following the sunnah, the Prophet's way: not only the prayers and fasts, but small things. Smiling, which a hadith calls charity. Helping at home, which 'A'isha said he did, serving his family. Greeting first. Eating with the right hand. The Qur'an uses uswah of Ibrahim, too. This week's lines, from Luqman to As-Sajdah, ran from Luqman's first advice and a mother's wahn, through a lowered voice and words that don't run out, to up in the night and joy kept hidden. And today: a beautiful example.
screen: `HEARTS REACHED THE THROATS.` · `USWATUN HASANAH.` · `CARRYING EARTH WITH THEM.` · `THE SUNNAH IN SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Choose one small, everyday thing the Prophet is reported to have done: smiling at the next person you meet, helping with a chore unasked, saying salam first, sitting down to drink, eating with the right hand and saying bismillah. Pick just one, and picture the moment in your day where it fits. If you're not Muslim, you can still pick one as a kindness worth trying.
Uswah. A model to copy; uswatun hasanah, the beautiful example the Qur'an names in the Prophet, in the middle of the trench. Today's word.
Your line: do the hard thing with them. An example is shown, not told. That closes the week.
